name: Reg.exe
description: Reg is a Windows utility used to interact with the Windows Registry. It can be used at the command-line interface to query, add, modify, and remove information. Utilities such as Reg are known to be used by persistent threats.
summary: Interact with and modify the Windows Registry of a local or remote system
Gather details from the Windows Registry of a local or remote system
Check for installed software on the system
Retrieve proxy information in the Registry

attack_relationships.description: During APT28 Nearest Neighbor Campaign, APT28 used the following commands to dump SAM, SYSTEM, and SECURITY hives: reg save hklm\sam, reg save hklm\system, and reg save hklm\security.

During Operation CuckooBees, the threat actors leveraged a custom tool to dump OS credentials and used following commands: `reg save HKLM\SYSTEM system.hiv`, `reg save HKLM\SAM sam.hiv`, and `reg save HKLM\SECURITY security.hiv`, to dump SAM, SYSTEM and SECURITY hives.
During Operation Digital Eye, threat actors used `reg save` to retrieve credentials from the Security Account Manager (SAM) database.

During Operation Wocao, the threat actors executed `/c cd /d c:\windows\temp\ & reg query HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\<username>\PuTTY\Sessions\` to detect recent PuTTY sessions, likely to further lateral movement.
BabyShark has executed the reg query command for HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Terminal Server Client\Default.
Epic uses the rem reg query command to obtain values from Registry keys.
HeartCrypt can use the `reg add` command via `cmd.exe` for Registry modification.
KeyBoy issues the command reg add “HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon” to achieve persistence.
PLAINTEE uses reg add to add a Registry Run key for persistence.
POWRUNER may query the Registry by running reg query on a victim.
PUBLOAD has queried Registry values to identify software using `reg query`.

The Gentlemen Ransomware has written registry keys within HKLM and HKCU to gain persistence device wide and to have redundancy. The Gentlemen Ransomware has added registry keys to maintain persistence through `reg add HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run /v GupdateS /t REG_SZ /d “<malware_path>” /f` and `reg add HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run /v GupdateU /t REG_SZ /d “<malware_path>” /f`.
Ursnif has used Reg to query the Registry for installed programs.
Zebrocy executes the reg query command to obtain information in the Registry.

attack_detection_strategies.name: Behavior-Based Registry Modification Detection on Windows

analytics.description: Behavior chain involving abnormal registry modifications via CLI, PowerShell, WMI, or direct API calls, especially targeting persistence, privilege escalation, or defense evasion keys, potentially followed by service restart or process execution. Such as editing Notify/Userinit/Startup keys, or disabling SafeDllSearchMode.

attack_detection_strategies.name: Detection of Registry Query for Environmental Discovery

analytics.description: Registry read access associated with suspicious or non-interactive processes querying system config, installed software, or security settings.

attack_detection_strategies.name: Detect Credential Discovery via Windows Registry Enumeration

analytics.description: Defenders observe command-line executions or API-based registry reads targeting sensitive paths like HKLM or HKCU with keyword filters such as 'password', 'cred', or 'logon'. Typically performed by Reg.exe, PowerShell, custom binaries, or offensive tools such as Cobalt Strike. Correlation with process ancestry and command-line arguments indicates suspicious credential discovery activity.

attack_detection_strategies.name: Credential Dumping from SAM via Registry Dump and Local File Access

analytics.description: An adversary running with SYSTEM-level privileges executes commands or accesses registry keys to dump the SAM hive or directly reads sensitive local files from the config directory. This behavior often involves sequential access to HKLM\SAM, HKLM\SYSTEM, and creation of .save or .dmp files, enabling offline hash extraction.

attack_detection_strategies.name: Detection Strategy for NTFS File Attribute Abuse (ADS/EAs)

analytics.description: Suspicious use of NTFS file attributes such as Alternate Data Streams (ADS) or Extended Attributes (EA) to hide data. Defender perspective: anomalous file creations or modifications containing colon syntax (file.ext:ads), API calls like ZwSetEaFile/ZwQueryEaFile, or PowerShell/Windows utilities interacting with -stream parameters. Correlation across file metadata anomalies, process lineage, and command execution provides context.

related_CVE.description: JetBrains TeamCity authentication bypass leading to remote code execution. A threat actor who exploited it used reg.exe to save the SYSTEM registry hive for credential dumping.

mitigations.name: Restrict Registry Permissions
mitigations.description: Ensure proper permissions are set for Registry hives to prevent users from modifying keys for system components that may lead to privilege escalation.

mitigations.name: Password Policies
mitigations.description: Do not store credentials within the Registry.

mitigations.name: Audit
mitigations.description: Proactively search for credentials within the Registry and attempt to remediate the risk.

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.description: If it is necessary that software must store credentials in the Registry, then ensure the associated accounts have limited permissions so they cannot be abused if obtained by an adversary.

mitigations.name: Password Policies
mitigations.description: Ensure that local administrator accounts have complex, unique passwords across all systems on the network.

mitigations.name: User Training
mitigations.description: Limit credential overlap across accounts and systems by training users and administrators not to use the same password for multiple accounts.

mitigations.name: Privileged Account Management
mitigations.description: Do not put user or admin domain accounts in the local administrator groups across systems unless they are tightly controlled, as this is often equivalent to having a local administrator account with the same password on all systems. Follow best practices for design and administration of an enterprise network to limit privileged account use across administrative tiers.

mitigations.name: Restrict File and Directory Permissions
mitigations.description: Consider adjusting read and write permissions for NTFS EA, though this should be tested to ensure routine OS operations are not impeded.
